name: LLD Core Rubric
_note: Eight criteria, each owned by exactly one evaluator at exactly one stage. Six are measured — from the class graph, the scenario walkthroughs, or the diff between the design before and after a requirement change. Two need reading and go to the LLM. An earlier draft had twelve criteria and they overlapped badly: one god class lost points under responsibilities, cohesion, abstraction and extensibility at once, so a single flaw read as four. Version 2 replaces the LLM-judged 'extensibility' with a measured 'change-resilience' and adds 'behaviour', which no static class diagram can score.

criteria.name: Requirement Coverage
criteria.question: Does the design account for what the brief actually asked for?

bands.0: Most requirements have nothing in the design that speaks to them.
bands.1: Under half the requirements are addressed.
bands.2: Most requirements are addressed, but several are missing.
bands.4: Every requirement is owned by something in the design.

criteria.name: Class Responsibilities
criteria.question: Does each class own one clear job?

bands.0: Several classes are doing many unrelated jobs, or the design is a list with no structure.
bands.1: One class absorbs most of the behaviour.
bands.2: One class is overloaded but the rest are focused.
bands.3: Responsibilities are mostly clean, with minor overlap.
bands.4: Every class describes a single job in one sentence.

criteria.name: Coupling and Cohesion
criteria.question: Do the relationships between classes hold together?

bands.0: Dangling references, cycles and orphans throughout.
bands.3: One minor fault, such as a single orphan.
bands.4: No orphans, cycles or dangling references.

criteria.name: Use of Abstraction
criteria.question: Is there a seam where this problem is known to change, and does it carry weight?

bands.0: No abstractions, or abstractions that nothing implements and no variation needs.
bands.2: Some variation points have seams; others are baked in.
bands.3: Nearly all variation points are behind an abstraction.
bands.4: Every declared variation point is behind an abstraction that something implements.

criteria.name: Behaviour
criteria.question: Does the design actually run its scenarios — every step on a class and method that exist?

bands.0: No scenario was walked, or most steps land on classes or methods the design does not declare.
bands.1: Only one scenario walked, or one class performs nearly every step.
bands.2: All scenarios walked, but steps dangle or a failure scenario ends as if nothing went wrong.
bands.3: Every step resolves; one minor issue such as a class no scenario ever exercises.
bands.4: Every scenario walked, every step on a declared class and method, failure paths present, work spread across the design.

criteria.name: Handling Change
criteria.question: When the requirements changed, did the design absorb it by adding, or by reopening what already worked?

bands.0: No revision, or nothing in the revised design owns the new behaviour.
bands.1: Absorbed by editing existing classes and adding a flag, a type field or a conditional.
bands.2: Absorbed only by editing existing classes — no flag, but working code was reopened.
bands.3: A new class was added, but two or more existing classes had to change too, or it extends a concrete class.
bands.4: A new class behind a seam that already existed; at most one existing class touched to wire it in.

criteria.name: Edge Cases and Assumptions
criteria.question: Were the gaps in the brief filled deliberately rather than silently?

bands.0: No assumptions recorded and no failure path considered.
bands.1: Assumptions recorded but nothing handles the unhappy path.
bands.2: Some thought given to failure, but the important cases are missing.
bands.3: Assumptions are explicit and the main failure paths are named.
bands.4: Assumptions are explicit and failure is modelled as part of the domain.

anchors.1: Assumptions: 'one vehicle per spot'. Nothing in any class or walkthrough says what happens when the lot is full.
anchors.3: Assumption 'entry is refused when nothing fits' and a walkthrough that ends `refused` with the class that decides it.
anchors.4: As 3, plus the refusal is a named type or result the caller has to handle, not a null.

criteria.name: Reasoning
criteria.question: Can the learner say what they chose, what they rejected, and defend it when pressed?

bands.0: No decisions recorded and probes left unanswered.
bands.1: Answers restate the design without reasoning, or dodge the question.
bands.2: Answers describe what the design does but not what it cost or what was rejected.
bands.3: Answers name a specific class and a consequence; at least one alternative is weighed.
bands.4: Answers name the class, the alternative rejected, why, and what would change their mind.

anchors.1: Q: 'Weekend rates arrive — what changes?' A: 'I would update the pricing.'
anchors.2: A: 'I would add a weekend rate to the fee calculation in ParkingLot.'
anchors.3: A: 'A WeekendPricing class implementing PricingStrategy; ParkingLot does not change because it only sees the interface.'
anchors.4: As 3, plus: 'I considered a rate table on Spot and rejected it because rates vary by time, not by location — if they started varying by floor I would revisit.'
